subtype: Approach: sleeping properly the night before and light revision [Thinking]
passage: Warden's log, Monday, exam week. Most boys in Room 4 were still up with torches at 11 pm, cramming for tomorrow's science exam. Deepak was not. At 8 pm he sat with only his one-page summary, read it through twice, and told Jeevan, his roommate, "If I stay up till twelve, I'll be yawning over the paper. I've studied all week. Tonight I sleep." Jeevan teased him, but Deepak had his light off by 9:30. At breakfast this morning he was the only one in Room 4 not rubbing his eyes. I'll share his routine at Wednesday's house meeting.

qa.q: What did Deepak read at 8 pm?
qa.a: Only his one-page summary, read through twice.

qa.q: What does Deepak's 'Tonight I sleep' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt calm and confident enough to trust a week of study, rather than anxious enough to cram.

qa.q: What could the other boys in Room 4 try before the next exam?
qa.a: A short summary revision in the evening and an early night like Deepak, instead of cramming with torches past eleven.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Deepak's choice by breakfast?
qa.a: Jeevan teased him at night, but seeing him fresh while others rub their eyes may make Jeevan wonder if Deepak was right.

grounding: Shows a boy reasoning that staying up late will make him drowsy, revising his summary early and sleeping by 9:30 to trust what he learned.

subtype: Approach: sleeping properly the night before and light revision [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday, 9:25 pm
Maths final tomorrow. Zeenat called at nine and said she's staying up till midnight doing every chapter again. For a second I panicked and pulled out my textbook. Then I remembered last term: I stayed up till one, and in the exam I read question 3 four times because my eyes kept closing. So no. I did my summary sheet at 8, formulas and the two tricky kinds of sums, and that's it. Mummy just looked in: "Amandeep puttar, lights off?" Yes. I've practised every day this week. I'm going to trust that. Goodnight, diary.

qa.q: When did Zeenat call?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Zeenat said she was staying up till midnight?
qa.a: Amandeep panicked for a moment and pulled out the textbook, then felt steadier remembering how sleepy the last late night had made him.

qa.q: What might make Amandeep's plan even stronger?
qa.a: Keeping the summary sheet handy for a quick look at breakfast instead of reopening the whole book; the early night is the main part.

qa.q: How might Zeenat's plan look next to Amandeep's the next morning?
qa.a: Zeenat may arrive having gone over every chapter but tired, while Amandeep arrives rested, so she might wonder which plan was better.

grounding: Illustrates a boy deciding not to stay up late before an exam, revising summary points in the evening and sleeping early to trust his preparation.

subtype: Approach: breaking division into smaller steps [Thinking]
passage: Long division made Afreen want to throw her pencil across their Hyderabad flat. 736 divided by 4, and the numbers kept sliding around the page. Her little sister Aadhya was colouring beside her. Afreen stared at the teacher's worked example and muttered, "What is it actually doing?" She traced it with her finger. "Divide... then multiply... then take away... then bring the next number down. Then again." Four moves, the same four every time. She wrote them in a column: D, M, S, B. Then she did ten tiny divides, ten multiplies, ten take-aways, one kind at a time. Only then did she try 736 again, saying each letter aloud. 184. It checked.

qa.q: What four letters did Afreen write in a column?
qa.a: D, M, S, B.

qa.q: How was Afreen feeling at the start, and what does her muttering show?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and confused, wanting to throw her pencil; muttering 'What is it actually doing?' shows her hunting for the pattern underneath.

qa.q: What else could Afreen try if one of the four steps keeps going wrong?
qa.a: Practise only that step a little more or ask her teacher to show that one move; breaking the sum into four is what made it manageable.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her sister's muttering?
qa.a: Aadhya is colouring beside her, so she may find the muttered letters odd or funny, not knowing they were cracking the sum.

grounding: Shows a child seeing that long division is four repeated steps, practising each alone, and then joining them to solve the sum.

subtype: Approach: breaking division into smaller steps [Thinking]
passage:
"Vaibhav, I hate this. 552 divided by 6 is impossible."
"What does the book do first?"
"It... goes 6 into 55."
"And then?"
Gopika squinted. "Then it multiplies. 6 times 9, 54. Then it takes away. 55 minus 54 is 1."
"And then?"
"Brings down the 2. Oh." She sat up. "It's the same four things. Divide, times, take away, bring down. Over and over."
"So which one's hard?"
"None of them, alone." She wrote four lines of just multiplying, then four of just subtracting. "Okay. Now together." Twelve. 6 into 12 is 2. "Ninety-two!"
Vaibhav checked. "92 times 6... 552. Yep."

qa.q: What did Gopika get for 552 divided by 6?
qa.a: Ninety-two.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel when she said 'Oh' and sat up?
qa.a: She felt surprised and excited, suddenly seeing that the confusing sum was the same four steps repeated 😊

qa.q: What could Gopika do tomorrow to make the method stick?
qa.a: Practise each step alone a few times, then do a couple of full sums while saying the four steps aloud.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see his part in this?
qa.a: Vaibhav only asked 'And then?', so he can see Gopika worked out the steps herself, and probably feels pleased to have helped quietly.

grounding: Illustrates a child realising long division is divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, practising each step alone and then combining them.

subtype: Approach: using an everyday example to understand fractions [Thinking]
passage:
Diary, Tuesday night
Fractions were a fog all week. Miss wrote 3/4 on the board and I only saw two numbers with a line. Tonight at dinner I told Ama I didn't get it. She took a hot roti, folded it, and tore it into four pieces on my plate. Then she took one back. "How much is left, Pema, my boy?" "Three pieces." "Out of?" "Four." And it clicked. Three out of four. The bottom number is how many pieces the roti was cut into, the top is how many I have! I ate my three-fourths very slowly. Tomorrow I'll tell Urmila, who sits next to me, because she was lost too.

qa.q: How many pieces did Ama tear the roti into?
qa.a: Four pieces.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when it clicked?
qa.a: Pema felt delighted and relieved after a foggy week, finally seeing what the top and bottom numbers mean.

qa.q: What other everyday things could Pema use to practise fractions?
qa.a: Cutting a fruit or folding paper into equal parts; real objects give the numbers a meaning he can hold.

qa.q: How might Urmila benefit from Pema's discovery?
qa.a: Urmila was lost too, so hearing about the roti could help her understand fractions the same way.

grounding: Shows a boy who cannot follow three-fourths until his mother tears a roti into four and takes one away, giving the number a real meaning.

subtype: Approach: using an everyday example to understand fractions [Thinking]
passage: At noon Ujjwal sat by the chulha in the courtyard, his slate on his knees. 3/4 still made no sense. "It's just a three sitting on a four," he complained to Asif, who had come over to eat. Ujjwal's mother flipped a roti off the tawa, laid it on his plate, and pressed the edge of her hand across it twice, making four pieces. She slid one onto Asif's plate. "How many are yours now?" "Three." "Out of how many?" Ujjwal looked from the roti to his slate. "Four. So the four is the whole roti in pieces, and the three is what I've got." He wiped the slate and drew a circle cut into four, shading three.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal sit with his slate?
qa.a: By the chulha in the courtyard.

qa.q: How was Ujjwal feeling about fractions before the roti?
qa.a: He was frustrated and confused, complaining that 3/4 was just a three sitting on a four.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next to check he really understands?
qa.a: Try 2/4 or 1/4 with the roti pieces, or draw them on his slate; if he can explain each, the idea has stuck.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Asif?
qa.a: Asif got an extra piece of roti and watched the lesson happen on the plate, so Asif may have learned fractions too.

grounding: Illustrates a boy grasping three-fourths when his mother cuts a roti into four and leaves him three, linking the number to real food.

subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
passage: In the small school at the edge of the village, Sarika could chant it faster than anyone: "Flip the second, then multiply!" She did twenty sums in the practice book, all correct. 3/4 ÷ 1/2, flip, multiply, done. Gurleen, her deskmate, asked, "But why do we flip?" Sarika shrugged. "Because that's the rule." On Friday Masterji wrote a new kind of question on the board: "A farmer has 3/4 of a field. Each plot is 1/8. How many plots?" Sarika stared. Where were the two fractions with the sign? There was no ÷ anywhere. She wrote nothing, and watched the chalk dust settle while the others slowly worked.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask Sarika?
qa.a: Gurleen asked, 'But why do we flip?'

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she stared at Masterji's question?
qa.a: She felt lost and helpless, because the rule she had chanted didn't tell her what to do without a ÷ sign.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Sarika learned?
qa.a: Answer Gurleen's question: work out why flipping works with a drawing, such as how many 1/8 plots fit in 3/4, so she can spot division in a new shape.

qa.q: How might Masterji see Sarika's empty page?
qa.a: Masterji would see that Sarika learned the rule without its meaning, since she was stuck the moment the usual sign disappeared.

grounding: Shows a girl who memorised 'flip and multiply' without understanding it, getting practice sums right but lost on a word problem in a new form.

subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
passage: In Leila's classroom in Toronto, dividing fractions had a song. "Keep, change, flip!" Leila sang it under her breath through every worksheet, and every answer came back with a check mark. At lunch Dalia asked how she got 3/2 for 1/2 divided by 1/3. "Keep, change, flip," Leila said. "Why does it work?" Leila bit her sandwich. "It just does." Then came the quiz. Question 4: 'A ribbon is 2/3 of a metre long. How many 1/6-metre pieces can you cut?' No division sign, no fractions lined up to flip. Leila read it three times, wrote '2/3 × 1/6?', crossed it out, and moved on, leaving an empty space.

qa.q: What song did Leila use for dividing fractions?
qa.a: 'Keep, change, flip!'

qa.q: What was Leila feeling as she crossed out her answer to Question 4?
qa.a: She felt confused and stuck, since the song didn't tell her the ribbon problem was a division.

qa.q: What else could Leila try so she understands, not only remembers?
qa.a: Draw the ribbon and count how many sixths fit into two-thirds; seeing why it works would help her spot division in new shapes.

qa.q: How might Dalia see Leila's 'It just does'?
qa.a: Dalia was curious why it works, so the answer may leave Dalia unconvinced that Leila really understands it.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who learned a rule for dividing fractions without knowing why, and is lost when a word problem comes in a new shape.

subtype: Approach: drawing pictures and diagrams of the idea [Action]
passage: Abhinav had read the plant chapter twice at the village school and still mixed up what roots and stems did. So after school he sat under the peepal tree with his notebook, a pencil stub, and a mustard plant his sister Aditi had pulled from the field. First he drew the roots, with all their tiny hairs. 'These drink water,' he wrote. Then the stem, with a thin tube up the middle: 'carries water up'. Then the leaves: 'make food with sunlight'. Drawing a leaf, he noticed lines running through it that he'd never read about. 'Veins?' he said. Aditi peered over. 'Like on your hand.' He added a label with a question mark, to ask Sir.

qa.q: What plant did Aditi pull from the field?
qa.a: A mustard plant.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt noticing the lines in the leaf?
qa.a: He seemed curious and interested, spotting a detail his reading had skipped and wanting to ask Sir about it.

qa.q: What else could Abhinav add to his drawing method?
qa.a: Cover the labels and try saying each part's job from memory; drawing already made him notice details reading missed.

qa.q: How does Aditi seem to see his drawing?
qa.a: Aditi peers over and links the veins to his hand, so she seems interested and happy to help.

grounding: Shows a boy drawing and labelling the roots, stem and leaves of a plant and noticing details his reading had skipped.

subtype: Approach: drawing pictures and diagrams of the idea [Action]
passage: Kwame's science teacher in Accra had given the class a page to read on plants, and Kwame had read it. But when Wei asked him what the stem does, he said, "Holds the plant up?" and wasn't sure. That evening he took a sheet of paper and a bean plant from his mother's garden pot. He drew the roots spreading like a net, then the stem, then three leaves, and wrote beside each what it does. Halfway through the leaves he stopped. The tiny holes underneath, the little tubes in the stem: none of that had stuck when he read. He went back to the page and found them. Next day he showed Wei the drawing, labels in red.

qa.q: Where did Kwame get the bean plant?
qa.a: From his mother's garden pot.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel when Wei asked what the stem does?
qa.a: He was unsure and a little embarrassed, since he had read the page but couldn't say for certain.

qa.q: What else could Kwame do before the test?
qa.a: Redraw the plant from memory and check it against his labelled drawing; drawing made him notice what reading skipped.

qa.q: How might Wei see Kwame's red-labelled drawing?
qa.a: Wei, who had asked about the stem, might find the drawing clear and want to use it to study too.

grounding: Illustrates a boy drawing and labelling the parts of a plant and noticing details that reading alone had let him skip.

subtype: Approach: trying easy examples first then harder ones [Action]
passage: I was doing my own homework on the diwan when Siddharth started fighting with decimals. He'd written 2.75 + 1.5 = 2.90, and the teacher had crossed it out. Dada Jagdish emptied his coin purse on the table. "Start small," he said. Siddharth took two fifty-paise coins. "Point five and point five... that's one rupee. One!" He grinned. Next he tried 1.5 plus 0.5 with coins: two. Then, slowly, he lined up 2.75 and 1.5 in his notebook, points under points, and wrote 4.25. He counted it out in coins to check. It matched. I don't know what clicked, but he did five more without the coins.

qa.q: What had Siddharth first written for 2.75 + 1.5?
qa.a: He'd written 2.90, and the teacher had crossed it out.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after getting 'One!' with the coins?
qa.a: His grin shows he felt pleased and more confident, ready to try a slightly bigger sum 🙂

qa.q: What could Siddharth try once the coins aren't needed?
qa.a: Harder sums on paper, going back to coins only if an answer looks wrong; building up in steps is what gave him confidence.

qa.q: How does Dada Jagdish seem to see the problem?
qa.a: Dada Jagdish sees that Siddharth needs to start small, so he offers coins that make decimals something to touch.

grounding: Shows a boy adding 0.5 and 0.5 with coins before moving on to 2.75 plus 1.5, each success building his confidence.

subtype: Approach: trying easy examples first then harder ones [Action]
passage:
Monday. Darshan couldn't see how 0.5 and 0.5 made anything. His friend Kunal tipped two fifty-paise coins into his palm. "Half a rupee each. How much?" Darshan pushed them together. "One rupee." He wrote 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 and underlined it twice.
Wednesday. Darshan tried 1.25 + 0.75 with coins from his tin box, then on paper. Two. He didn't need the coins for the next three sums.
Friday. The class test had 2.75 + 1.5. Darshan lined up the points, added, and wrote 4.25. He sat back, smiling, and turned to the harder page.

qa.q: What did Darshan try with coins on Wednesday?
qa.a: He tried 1.25 + 0.75 with coins from his tin box.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling on Friday when he sat back smiling?
qa.a: He felt confident and proud, because the small wins with coins had prepared him for 2.75 + 1.5.

qa.q: Why did starting with coins work better than jumping straight to the test sums?
qa.a: Each easy success showed him decimals made sense, so he trusted himself to try the next, bigger size.

qa.q: How might Kunal see his coin trick working?
qa.a: Kunal only tipped two coins into Darshan's palm, so seeing him move on to harder sums may make Kunal feel pleased to have helped.

grounding: Illustrates a boy moving from 0.5 plus 0.5 with coins to 2.75 plus 1.5 over a week, each success giving him confidence for the next.

subtype: Approach: deciding he is just bad at the subject and giving up [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday
Maths practice today. I got question 1 wrong. Then question 2. Then question 3. Madhav, next to me, got all three right and didn't even look worried. That's when I decided. I'm not a maths person. Some girls are, and I'm just not. So I closed the book and drew flowers in the margin for the rest of the period. Miss asked, "Jasleen, why did you stop?" and I said I'm bad at maths, which is true. At home I didn't do the practice sheet either. What's the point? Madhav says he practised every evening last week. Probably he's just born good at it.

qa.q: What did Jasleen draw for the rest of the period?
qa.a: Flowers in the margin.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel after the third wrong answer?
qa.a: Jasleen felt discouraged and defeated, deciding she's 'not a maths person' and closing the book.

qa.q: What would you change first for Jasleen?
qa.a: Treat the three wrong answers as clues, go over one with Miss, and do the practice sheet; stopping practice is what keeps her stuck.

qa.q: How might Madhav's success look different from how Jasleen sees it?
qa.a: Madhav practised every evening last week, so his right answers may come from practice, not from being born good at it.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after three wrong answers, decides she is not a maths person and stops practising, the very thing that would help.

subtype: Approach: deciding he is just bad at the subject and giving up [Pitfall]
passage: In the kasba school, Masterji called Nazia up to the blackboard three times that week. Three sums, three wrong answers, and each time the back rows giggled. On the walk home past the sugarcane fields, she kicked a stone. "I'm just not a maths person," she told Omkar, her cousin. "Abba wasn't either." "Masterji gave us extra sums for Sunday," Omkar said. "I'm not doing them. What's the use?" On Sunday Omkar sat on the charpai with his sums, stuck, then unstuck. Nazia sat at the other end, plaiting grass. By Monday, the sums on the board looked even stranger to her.

qa.q: How many times did Masterji call Nazia to the blackboard that week?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she kicked the stone?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and defeated after three wrong answers and the giggling, enough to give up.

qa.q: What could help Nazia instead of giving up?
qa.a: Doing the Sunday sums alongside Omkar and asking Masterji about one wrong answer; practice is exactly what the belief was stopping.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Nazia plaiting grass on Sunday?
qa.a: Omkar gets stuck and unstuck on his own sums, so he may see that she is missing the practice that helps him.

grounding: Illustrates a girl deciding after three wrong answers that she is not a maths person, skipping practice, and falling further behind.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. For a week Kishore has been guessing at subtraction and getting a different answer each time. Today he came to my desk with a torn slip of paper. On it he had written: 'I get lost in the borrowing step, when the top number is smaller.' Then: 'Can you show only that part again?' I did, with bundles of ten sticks, breaking one bundle open when the ones ran out. He did 52 − 27 at my desk and got 25. Sachin, who was hovering nearby, asked if he could watch too. Kishore's slip is going on the wall as an example of a good question.

qa.q: What did Kishore write on the slip of paper?
qa.a: 'I get lost in the borrowing step, when the top number is smaller.'

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when he brought the slip to the desk?
qa.a: He was probably a little nervous but determined, after a week of frustrating guesses.

qa.q: What made Kishore's question work so well?
qa.a: It named the exact step, borrowing, so the teacher could show just that part instead of the whole topic again.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Kishore's slip?
qa.a: The note-writer sees it as a model of a good question and is putting it on the wall for others.

grounding: Shows a child who notices guessing isn't working, writes down that the borrowing step is where he gets lost, and asks the teacher to show that step.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
passage:
Friday
For days I've been guessing on subtraction. 403 minus 168, and a new answer every time. Last night I did one sum very slowly and wrote down where my head went blank. It was the same place every time: the 3 on top is smaller than the 8, and next door is a 0, so where do I borrow from? I wrote in the back of my notebook: 'Borrowing across a zero: please show again.' Today I gave it to Sir. He did just that step on the board, twice. 403 − 168 = 235. I got it. Imran had said just copy his answers, but Mummy said, 'Harish beta, copying won't sit the exam for you.'

qa.q: What did Harish write in the back of his notebook?
qa.a: 'Borrowing across a zero: please show again.'

qa.q: How did Harish feel about the days of guessing?
qa.a: Harish seemed frustrated at getting a new answer each time, which pushed him to find exactly where he got lost.

qa.q: Why did writing down the stuck step help more than guessing?
qa.a: It pinned down the one step, borrowing across a zero, so Sir could show just that instead of the whole topic.

qa.q: How might Sir see Harish's note?
qa.a: Sir can see exactly what to teach and did that step twice on the board, so he likely appreciated such a clear question.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who stops guessing, writes down that borrowing across a zero is where he gets lost, and asks the teacher to show that step again.

subtype: Approach: watching a video explanation and copying the method [Action]
passage: The tablet's battery showed fifteen percent, the internet in Ayesha's building kept buffering, and a wedding band was thumping below the window. Still, the angles lesson was only eight minutes long. Ayesha pressed play. "Step one: put the centre of the protractor on the corner." Pause. She did it in her notebook. "Step two: line up the zero with one arm." Pause. She lined it up. "Read the scale that starts at zero." Pause. 65 degrees. She played on; the teacher on screen said 65. Yes. Dilnaz, her older sister, plugged in the charger just as the screen dimmed. "Keep going," she said. Ayesha measured two more before the video froze again.

qa.q: How long was the angles lesson?
qa.a: Only eight minutes long.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when the video showed 65 too?
qa.a: She felt pleased and more confident that her method matched, so she carried on despite the buffering.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha do if the video keeps freezing?
qa.a: Write each step in her notebook as she goes, so she can keep practising from her own notes without the video.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz seem to see Ayesha's effort?
qa.a: Dilnaz plugs in the charger and says 'Keep going', so she seems supportive and wants her to finish.

grounding: Shows a girl pausing a short video lesson on angles after each step, repeating it in her notebook and checking her answer against the video.

subtype: Approach: watching a video explanation and copying the method [Action]
passage: Lakshmi had the family tablet for twenty minutes before her brother Akash's turn, so she chose a short lesson on types of angles. Sitting cross-legged on the floor of their Chennai flat, she paused after every step. The teacher drew a right angle; Lakshmi drew one in her notebook and wrote '90°'. Pause. An acute angle; she drew a thin one and wrote 'less than 90'. Pause. Then an example: which kind is 135°? Lakshmi wrote 'obtuse' before pressing play, and the video said obtuse. She punched the air. Akash, waiting on the sofa, said, "You're pausing every ten seconds!" "That's how it goes in," Lakshmi said.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi write for 135°?
qa.a: She wrote 'obtuse'.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi punch the air?
qa.a: She felt excited and proud that her answer matched the video before it told her 🎉

qa.q: What would help Lakshmi if the video still moved too fast?
qa.a: Rewatching a step and copying it again, or writing a short list of angle types to test herself later.

qa.q: How does Akash see Lakshmi's way of watching?
qa.a: Akash, waiting for his turn, finds all the pausing slow and a bit annoying.

grounding: Illustrates a girl watching a video lesson on angles, pausing to repeat each step in her notebook and checking her answer against it.

subtype: Approach: leaving it and returning after a rest [Revision]
passage: Last week a triangle problem nearly beat me. Find the missing angle, with two sides marked equal. I stared at it for twenty minutes. My answer kept coming out as 140°, which can't be right in a triangle that already has a 70° angle. My head felt like wet cotton. Then the boys downstairs shouted for football, and I just went. I played for half an hour. When I came back, sweaty, and looked at the drawing again, I saw it at once: I had marked the wrong two sides as equal. I fixed the labels and finished in five minutes. Minakshi Aunty, passing the door, said, 'Pema beta, see? Your brain needed air.'

qa.q: How long did Pema play football?
qa.a: Half an hour.

qa.q: How did Pema feel after twenty minutes of staring?
qa.a: Pema felt foggy and frustrated, with a head 'like wet cotton' and an answer that couldn't be right.

qa.q: What could Pema try next time he's stuck like this?
qa.a: Take a short break sooner, then check the labels first; the rest let him see the mistake he'd been staring past.

qa.q: How does Minakshi Aunty see what happened?
qa.a: Minakshi Aunty thinks his brain simply needed air, so she sees the break as part of solving it, not time wasted.

grounding: Shows a boy who stares at a geometry problem for twenty minutes, goes out to play, and on returning spots his mislabelled sides and finishes quickly.

subtype: Approach: leaving it and returning after a rest [Revision]
passage: Tuition note, Friday. Rafiq sat over one geometry question for twenty minutes today, the one with the parallelogram. He kept writing and rubbing out, and his perimeter kept coming out too small. Then he pushed back his chair and asked if he could throw the ball with Pranav in the yard for ten minutes. I said yes. When he came back and looked at his drawing, he said, 'Oh! I called this side 6 and it's the 9 one.' He relabelled the sides and finished in five minutes. I'm going to suggest short breaks to the whole group when someone is stuck this long.

qa.q: Which shape was in Rafiq's geometry question?
qa.a: A parallelogram.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have felt when he said 'Oh!'?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and relieved, suddenly seeing he had swapped the 6 and 9 sides.

qa.q: What does this suggest for other students who get stuck?
qa.a: A short break after a long stuck spell can help them return and spot mistakes, like a wrong label, that staring missed.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Rafiq's break?
qa.a: The note-writer saw it work so well that short breaks will now be suggested to the whole group.

grounding: Illustrates a boy leaving a puzzling geometry problem for a break outside and, on returning, seeing he mislabelled the sides and finishing quickly.
